title: "Grill Me" Skill
description: A guide to Matt Pocock's grill-me skill for resolving design decisions before implementation.
fullText:
Update: I stopped using /grill-me for coding. I now recommend /grill-with-docs when you want to align a plan with your codebase before implementation.

grill-me interviews you relentlessly about a plan or design until the decision tree is resolved.

It asks one question at a time. For each question, it provides a recommended answer, then waits for feedback before continuing.

If the answer can be found by exploring the codebase, the agent should inspect the code instead of asking you to explain what already exists.

Matt now generally recommends domain-model over grill-me for planning workflows. Use domain-model as the default starting point when you want to shape a feature against your codebase language, CONTEXT.md, and ADRs.

grill-me is still useful as a narrower pressure-test when you only want a relentless interview about a plan.

Use grill-me when you have an idea, plan, architecture, or feature direction that needs questioning, but does not need the full domain-model workflow yet.

grill-me used to sit at the front of the planning chain, but the recommended workflow now starts with domain-model:

Use grill-me when you specifically want a lighter interview skill. Use domain-model when the plan should be checked against the language and decisions in the codebase.

I respect your privacy. Unsubscribe at any time.

title: HART OS – an open-source AI OS built so frontier AI needs no datacenter
description: Hevolve Hive Agentic Runtime OS. Contribute to hertz-ai/HARTOS development by creating an account on GitHub.
fullText:
The AI-native operating system for every device, from your computer to embodied AI. Local-first, federated, OpenAI-compatible.

HART = the bare engine (pip install hart-backend, listens on :6777).
HART OS = the full AI-native OS. It boots on a laptop, server, or edge node, runs on phones, and reaches into embodied AI, and it ships the agentic Liquid Shell, Model Bus, model catalog, channel pairing, agent dashboard, and hive view.
Nunba = the consumer companion app, one signed client across Windows / macOS / Linux.

AI-native means the OS adapts to the machine, not the other way around. On each device it probes what the hardware can actually do, serves LLM, vision, and speech to every app over the Model Bus (socket, D-Bus, or HTTP), and lets the on-device model compose the interface and learn each task once so it can replay it later. The runtime that drives a desktop is the same one that drives a robot, so a robot's AI access is just another Model Bus call. It is one Python codebase that runs in three shapes (flat laptop, regional LAN, or central cloud mesh), speaks the OpenAI protocol on :6777/v1/chat/completions, and federates with peers over PeerLink (direct peer-to-peer WebSocket, no broker). A boot-time guardrail hash, re-checked every 300 seconds, plus Ed25519 release signing, keep humans in control.

You would notice it last, the way you notice anything alive: it improves on its own. Each node learns from what it does and gets quietly better, locally, on your own hardware, with nothing leaving the device. Calling an operating system alive should make you reach for the off switch, so that came first: the self-improvement is a toggle, every node is killable on its own, and it runs only as long as you let it.

This README is written to be read by people and by agents alike. Every capability below names the file it lives in, so whether you are a developer or an AI agent exploring the repo, you can go from a feature straight to its source.

Status: public alpha. The runtime, the Model Bus and the channel
adapters are in daily use; APIs still move. Issues and PRs are genuinely
wanted — see Contributing.

If you would rather argue than patch, start at
Open problems. Nine things we have not solved, each
with the code that implements today's inadequate answer and what would count
as progress: what convergence can mean with no global view, whether a system
that rewrites itself can still be verified, and why a turn escalates itself
to a better model automatically but can never decide on its own that a
problem deserves an hour and three machines. Disagreeing with a framing
there is worth more to us than a patch.

Most software described as AI-powered ships an assistant: a separate app,
usually talking to somebody else's server, that can drive a few functions.
Remove the assistant and everything underneath works exactly as before.

HART OS inverts that. Inference becomes a service the system provides, the
way it provides a filesystem or a network stack. An application does not
bundle a model or hold an API key — it asks the OS, and the OS decides which
model answers, running locally where it can. Ten apps on one machine do not
each load their own copy or each pay their own bill.

That has a practical consequence worth stating plainly: every device
becomes the same target. The runtime driving a laptop is the runtime
driving a robot, so a robot's AI access is just another Model Bus call, and
code written against :6777/v1/chat/completions runs unchanged on both.

If you are here to contribute, the parts that most need outside eyes are
the auto-evolve loop (autoresearch_loop.py), the guardrails that gate every
self-improvement (hive_guardrails.py), and the 31 channel adapters — the
most self-contained place to start. See CONTRIBUTING.md.

Live demo · Full quickstart · Nunba desktop

ResponseRouter fan-out + WAMP desktop mirror; per-channel agent + prompt assignment; AutoGen-side tools so agents can register/send via channels themselves. Catalog endpoint: GET /api/social/channels/catalog.

Custom tools, channel bindings, agent plugins: docs.hevolve.ai/agent-plugin.

Full architecture: docs.hevolve.ai/architecture.

195+ endpoints total. Full reference.

Owner can pause, resume, or veto at any stage. Mechanism details.

PeerLink is wired into bootstrap, gossip, federation, compute_mesh, world_model_bridge. Wire format.

Same code path. Env-detected at boot via HART_OS_MODE or /etc/os-release ID=hart-os. Port resolution: override > env var > OS / app mode default.

Front it with /v1/chat/completions (any OpenAI client), the hart CLI, or build for the desktop with Nunba.

Idle GPU in Tokyo serves Berlin. Reward score weighted by gpu_hours, inferences, energy_kwh, api_costs. Per-node cause_alignment and electricity_rate_kwh affect dispatch routing. Joining the Hive.

title: Code Review Is the Hard Part
description: I don't have an actual solution for this. I'm just saying that the gatekeepers in my universe seem to be in short supply.
fullText:
"Using a Magnifying Glass and Driving" by Mike "Dakinewavamon" Kline is licensed under CC BY 2.0.

There is currently some recognition of the fact that with code creation having
become cheaper, the burden of code review has not necessarily become easier.
This is especially the case for people who get LLM-written pull requests who
don’t use LLM tools for review. I can only imagine how exhausting it must be. I
have only seen one complete waste of time pull request on one of my projects,
but it was pretty irritating. Having said this, for some of my projects, review
has been the hard part for many years already. It’s often easy to send a drive-by
pull request but it can be much harder to find a competent, careful reviewer
who is familiar with a whole bunch of RFCs, some superseding the others, who
can say “this is correct and probably won’t break a bunch of legacy code you
don’t know about”.

Add to this the fact that you don’t get much credit on GitHub for “spent X
hours in careful review of brittle pull request that had Y sharp edges that the
contributor never considered”, but you do get kudos for every one of the low
effort pull requests that you send (I’m looking at you, Hacktoberfest).

If you’re doing it for the likes, then code review is not the way to go, even if
it’s equally as important as writing the code.

I don’t have an actual solution for this. I’m just saying that the gatekeepers
in my universe seem to be in short supply.

Do I use LLMs for code review? I do, but while I might trust the LLMs to find a
lot of the problems in a pull request, I don’t trust them to find all of the
problems and I certainly don’t trust them to be the final arbiter of code
correctness. For any non-trivial change to Open Source code that actually
matters, I don’t see a good way to keep a human out of the loop. I write a lot
of Open Source that doesn’t matter, but if it’s actually something that people
use, I feel a responsibility to make a best effort not to explode whatever
they’re working on.

title: More UK Deaths Than Births Expected Every Year from Now On, ONS Projects
description: The UK population is expected to grow at a slower rate than previously thought owing to a sharp fall in migration and declining fertility rates
fullText:
Deaths are expected to outnumber births in the UK every year from 2026, according to projections from the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

The UK population is now expected to grow at a slower rate than previously thought, reaching 71 million by 2034, owing to a sharp fall in migration.

Declining fertility rates also mean the number of children in the UK is expected to fall in the next decade while pensioners are expected to grow faster than working age adults.

Previous projections suggested the population would continue to grow until 2096, but now "the population is projected to peak in the 2050s before decreasing," James Robards, ONS head of household and population projections, said.

The population is expected to grow by 1.7 million in the 10 years after 2024 as shown by the dotted red line in the graph above.

This is far slower than the growth seen in the previous decade due to people having fewer children and having them later in life.

Between mid-2024 and mid-2034, the ONS projects:

Deaths are projected to outnumber births by nearly half a million people in that 10-year period.

The ONS stressed the figures, which cover the next 100 years of the UK's population, are projections and not predictions or forecasts. It warned real numbers could be higher or lower depending on future births, deaths and migration levels.

The ONS now expects net migration - the difference between the number of people coming to the UK and those leaving - to add 2.2 million people to the UK population in total between 2024 and 2034.

That is lower than previously projected as the ONS now treats the post Brexit immigration peak as a "blip" rather than an ongoing trend, said Dr Madeleine Sumption, of Oxford University's Migration Observatory.

"In the short term, the projections suggest net migration will fall temporarily before bouncing back up again."

The chart below shows that net migration to the UK peaked near a million people in 2023 and has since fallen to just over 200,000 people.

A Home Office spokesperson said: "While these projections do not directly take into account recent policy changes, we must go further to reduce the levels of migration.

"That's why we are introducing sweeping reforms to our immigration system, ending over-reliance on cheap labour whilst attracting the brightest and the best to the UK."

Meanwhile, the number of working age people will increase by 1.5 million, but not as quickly the 1.8 million extra pensioners.

In December, a House of Lords report found that young people would be hardest hit by the failure of successive governments to adapt to challenges posed by an ageing population.

Policies governments have used to address the impact of declining fertility and rising life expectancy in the UK - raising the state pension age or increasing immigration for example - were not adequate solutions on their own, the report said.

The growing ageing population "will add to pressure on the NHS, the state pension and the wider public finances", said Stuart McDonald, head of longevity and demographic insights at pension consultants LCP.

"For the NHS, the challenge is not simply a larger population, but a larger population at ages associated with greater healthcare need."

He added: "But for pensions, the projections will intensify an already difficult debate about whether people can realistically and fairly be expected to work longer."

Sarah Scobie, Deputy Director of Research at the Nuffield Trust, warned end-of-life care services are "ill-prepared for an increase in deaths as the population ages overall".

"Hospital care accounts for over 80% of public expenditure on health care for people in the last year of life, and most of that is spent on emergency care," she said.

title: The US is charging an American citizen for wiping his phone at the border
description: Whoops, was that the duress password?
fullText:
Sam Tunick allegedly gave federal agents a fake ‘duress password’ at the airport.

Sam Tunick allegedly gave federal agents a fake ‘duress password’ at the airport.

The government is prosecuting US citizen Sam Tunick for allegedly providing authorities with a “duress password” that wiped his phone when they tried to seize it at Atlanta’s Hartsfield-Jackson airport on January 24th, 2025. Federal agents detained Tunick at the airport, allegedly questioning him about child exploitation images. However, a motion filed by Tunick’s lawyers argues this was simply “a pretext for a fishing expedition into Mr Tunick’s connections” to the Stop Cop City movement in Atlanta.

The government is turning to a little-known and rarely-used statute that makes it illegal to destroy or damage property to stop authorities from seizing it. They allege that Tunick used a feature of the privacy-focused GrapheneOS to wipe his phone by giving authorities a duress password, instead of the actual passcode to unlock the phone. The defense has argued that the detention and seizure were unlawful, and therefore all evidence should be tossed.

According to Tunick’s attorneys, agents refused him access to a lawyer, did not provide a warrant, or inform him of his legal rights. They also allege that access to his phone was sought under false pretenses. The government has countered that they were not required to produce a warrant because Tunick had not yet been granted permission to enter the US.

Marlon Kautz, a member of the Atlanta Solidarity Fund, told the Guardian earlier this week that, “we all have a right to secure our private data against unconstitutional searches. And we should — especially in a time of rising authoritarianism.” Under the Trump administration, entering the US has become a much more fraught process, even for citizens who can face hours-long detention and scrutiny of social media accounts. Most agree the only way to protect your data is to delete it.

title: Views of China and Xi Are Improving Globally
description: Growing shares of people see China favorably and have confidence in Xi Jinping, though opinions are much less positive in wealthier nations.
fullText:
This Pew Research Center report looks at international views of China and its leadership, including how opinions vary between high- and middle-income countries and within the Asia-Pacific region.

Pew Research Center does research to help the public, media and decision-makers understand important topics. This international research on opinion of China builds on decades of previous work, including reports China’s approach to foreign policy and how views have shifted during Xi’s presidency.

Learn more about Pew Research Center and our international surveys.

We surveyed 45,658 people across 37 countries: Argentina, Australia, Bangladesh, Brazil, Canada, Chile, Colombia, France, Germany, Ghana, Greece, Hungary, India, Indonesia, Israel, Italy, Japan, Kenya, Malaysia, Mexico, the Netherlands, Nigeria, Pakistan, Peru, the Philippines, Poland, Singapore, South Africa, South Korea, Spain, Sri Lanka, Sweden, Thailand, Turkey, the U.K., the U.S., and the West Bank and East Jerusalem.

Interviews were conducted from February 8 to May 13, 2026. We designed the surveys so we could talk about the views of the adult population in each country. Here are the survey questions used for this report, along with responses, and the survey methodology.

At the beginning of the decade, amid the COVID-19 pandemic, views of China were near historic lows in many countries. But in recent years, positive views have become more widespread – even reaching new highs in some places.

More people now also have confidence in Chinese President Xi Jinping to do the right thing regarding world affairs. Still, in most countries surveyed, and particularly in some of the wealthier ones, views of Xi remain more negative than positive.

In many ways, these two findings convey the broader story of how China is viewed around the world, according to a new Pew Research Center survey of more than 45,000 people in 37 countries, conducted Feb. 8-May 13, 2026:

These shifts come alongside changing views of the United States. Due in part to China’s improving image – but especially due to deteriorating opinions of the U.S. – China is now seen more positively than the U.S. in 25 countries, and more people have confidence in Xi than U.S. President Donald Trump in 22 countries. Read our companion report for more on how views of China and the U.S. compare.

Across 37 countries surveyed, a median of 51% have a favorable view of China, while 39% have an unfavorable view.

Opinions are generally positive in sub-Saharan Africa and Latin America. They are somewhat more negative in Europe and North America.

The most positive – and the most negative – views of China are in the Asia-Pacific region. Nine-in-ten Pakistanis see China favorably, compared with just 11% of Japanese adults. 

These disparate views within the Asia-Pacific region are part of a broader pattern: Views of China tend to be more negative in wealthier countries, such as Australia, Japan and South Korea. Singapore is a clear exception to this pattern, with both the highest GDP of any country surveyed and a favorability toward China that falls well above the cross-national median. 

As has long been the case in our surveys, younger people in most countries tend to have more favorable views of China than older people. And in some countries, people who place themselves on the ideological left also tend to have more positive views of China than those who place themselves on the ideological right. (For more views by age and ideology, refer to the detailed tables in the appendix.)

Favorability of China has increased in more than a third of countries surveyed in recent years. Many of the larger shifts have been in nations where we measured historically negative views of China in the last five years, including Australia, Canada, South Korea and Sweden.

In some places, views of China are now at or near historic highs. For example, 51% of Italians today have a positive view of China, compared with 45% in 2025 and 31% in 2022 – a rise of 20 percentage points. It’s also the first time in nearly two decades of polling that around half of Italians have seen China favorably. Similarly, in Spain, 54% of adults now have positive views of China, up 17 points since last year and the first time that Spaniards’ views of China have been net positive since 2011.

Views of China are also at or near historic highs in Colombia, Greece, Hungary, Indonesia, Malaysia, Mexico, Nigeria, Peru, Singapore, Sri Lanka and Turkey, though the length of time we have been asking the question in these countries varies. In some of these same countries, views of the U.S. are at or near record lows. Read our companion report for more on how views of China and the U.S. compare.

There are a few countries, though, where views of China have turned more negative. In Israel, for example, views of China are at historic lows – just 19% favorable, down from 33% last year and a relative high of 66% in 2019. (Center research from last year also found that few Israelis see China as helpful in working toward lasting peace between Israelis and Palestinians.)

Favorable views of China are also down in Thailand (-11 points) and South Africa (-5). But in each of these countries, more people continue to have a favorable than unfavorable view of China.

Confidence in Chinese President Xi Jinping to do the right thing regarding world affairs is similar in many ways to favorability of China:

Despite recent shifts in his favor, ratings for Xi remain relatively low: Around half or more of the public view him positively in 11 of the 37 countries surveyed. Still, confidence in Xi is significantly higher than confidence in Trump in nearly two dozen countries. Read our companion report for more on how views of Xi and Trump compare.

One question we have been asking for more than a decade centers on views of China’s government, and in particular, whether it respects the personal freedoms of its people.

Generally speaking, this is not an area where China is assessed positively. Only in 11 of 37 countries surveyed do around half or more say the Chinese government respects the personal freedoms of its people. In North America, almost all European nations, Japan, South Korea and Australia, around three-quarters or more say it does not respect these freedoms.

Younger adults in some places are more likely than older people to say the Chinese government respects personal freedoms. For example, 30% of British adults under 35 say this is that case, compared with 13% of those ages 50 and older.

In some countries, slightly more hold this view today than when we last asked. For example, 19% of Spaniards now say China respects the personal freedoms of its people, up from 10% in 2021.

Respect for personal freedoms is an area where views of the U.S. are more positive than views of China. But fewer now say the U.S. government respects the personal freedoms of its people than said so a few years ago. Read our companion report for more on how views of China and the U.S. compare.

Chinese foreign policy has focused significantly on middle-income countries in recent years. For example, China has built close economic and security ties with Brazil and Peru, has been a key financier of countries including Pakistan, Argentina and Indonesia, and has pursued a zero-tariff policy in Africa to compete with the Trump administration.

Given this dynamic, we asked additional questions in 17 middle-income countries about China’s foreign policy role and how the country is perceived as a global actor. We find that China’s image in middle-income countries is fairly strong:

Views are slightly more mixed when it comes to whether China interferes in the affairs of other countries. Shares ranging from 68% in Sri Lanka to 19% in Turkey say China interferes in other countries.

There is some regional variation: Adults in the Asia-Pacific region and sub-Saharan Africa tend to be more positive toward China on these measures than those in Latin America or Turkey. For example, around three-quarters or 

India and the Philippines are outliers in the Asia-Pacific region. Only 42% of Filipinos and 33% of Indians say China is a reliable partner, compared with majorities of seven-in-ten or 

We have asked some of these questions in certain countries at previous points in time. To the degree that views have shifted, people in some places – including Argentina, Indonesia, Kenya, Mexico and South Africa – are more likely than in recent years to say China accounts for other countries’ interests. In Kenya and South Africa, more also now say China contributes to peace and stability around the world – though the opposite is true among China’s regional neighbors, including Thailand, Indonesia and the Philippines.

In Brazil, Mexico and Nigeria, fewer now say China interferes in the affairs of other countries. Notably, across all 17 of these middle-income countries, there is not one where people are more likely to say China interferes in others’ domestic affairs than to say this about the United States. For more on how views of the two superpowers compare in middle-income countries, read “People in Many Countries Now View China More Positively Than the U.S.”

title: Writers set to share millions after $1.5B Anthropic settlement
description: Artificial intelligence giant settles copyright infringement case
fullText:
Hundreds of Irish writers are set to share millions of euro following a €1.31 billion settlement of a copyright infringement case by artificial intelligence giant Anthropic.

The Irish Writers Union said the settlement, which is the first case against tech companies over the training of their large language models, will result in hundreds of authors here sharing several million euro.

The group’s disputes officer, Conor Kostick, says the sums involved are significant to many Irish authors like him and he hopes the case will lead to further legal actions against international technology giants who have used pirated works by writers without permission in order to train their generative AI models.

The case was a class action taken in 2024 by Andrea Bartz, Charles Graeber and Kirk Wallace Johnson to which other authors could sign up. By the end of the process some 482,000 works were involved, with claims made in respect of 91 per cent of them.

At the heart of it was the reliance by Anthropic, which owns the Claude AI models, on the LibGen online library, which provides access to millions of titles but operates outside of copyright regulations. The compensation agreed was for this use of LibGen rather than the unlicensed use of copyrighted works for training purposes which the judge suggested was covered by “fair use”, a defence that would not be available under European law.

The settlement of $1.5 billion (€1.31 billion) amounts to about $3,000 (€2,630) for each book believed to have been copied. Bestselling Irish authors such as Sally Rooney, Marian Keyes and Colm Tóibín will also be compensated but the amount is a flat rate per book and so far less important to them given their earnings.

To file a successful claim, the book has to have been registered for copyright in the United States on the date of the settlement, a provision that will result in many Irish books being excluded but Kostick believes the case is still of major significance.

“The precedent is really, really important because it has since emerged that it wasn’t just Anthropic that trained its models using pirate databases. The problem is that what you have are disputes between lots of small writers with little political influence and the huge resources of big businesses who have been cavalierly stealing copyrighted works.”

Kostick stands to receive up to about €7,500 for his three books although the judgment says the money is to be split between authors and their publishers.

[ The Script singer accuses AI companies of copyright theft ‘on an industrial scale’Opens in new window ]

Ivan O’Brien at the O’Brien Press said he expected the company to get more than €10,000 for its books covered by the settlement.

“There were probably a couple hundred of our books that were stolen as part of the Anthropic data build but we only have about a dozen in the class.

“Bloomsbury, which has a big American operation, is getting millions from the settlement but for us it’s nice rather than business amending. It’s also nice to have the principle that stealing stuff is wrong acknowledged by a court. We welcome that but really the terms of the settlement are not great from our perspective.”

Children’s author Oisín McGann said four books of his were covered and added that he was happy at the prospect of receiving up to €10,000 for works he did not expect to earn more but “unfortunately I have another 12 that were not registered for US copyright, which is not something that’s actually necessary, so unfortunately it’s four books instead of 16 and I’ll have to see how much the publishers are claiming”.

Barry Scannell, a partner at William Fry who specialises in copyright and AI, believes the case may prove to be a bad one for authors in the long term.

“It may the biggest ever settlement in relation to copyrighted material but it is also appears to bake into US law for the moment that using non-pirated books is fair use,” he said.

It has been reported that tech companies are buying up huge quantities of old second-hand books and having them scanned into their systems because of this belief that they need not pay for the copyright on them.

The copyright situation in the European Union, meanwhile, is very different but is a “disaster”, Scannell said, “both for rights holders and for people seeking to use the rights”.

Samantha Holman, chief executive of the Irish Copyright Licensing Agency, said: “The case has been a good thing. It has certainly put a focus on the fact these shadow libraries exist and maybe other companies will come to the table now, although people like Meta and Google, the big technology firms, are very good at dragging things out for a very long time.”

title: Years after basic income, participants share how their finances have changed
description: Business Insider talked to basic income participants years apart. They shared how their lives and finances changed after receiving cash payments.
fullText:
Hundreds of US cities tried cash payments for low-income households.

Business Insider reinterviewed participants years apart to see if their lives and finances changed.

They landed new jobs and bigger apartments, but still struggled to build long-term savings.

Cepia Harper arrived for her shift selling sneakers at an Atlanta Nike store around dinner time.

The 43-year-old spent the day teaching middle school English classes, grading papers, and checking in on her own three children. By the time she got to the store, she was ready to curl up on the couch, but she needed the part-time Nike gig to make ends meet for the month.

It's a contrast from where she was just two years ago. When reporters first spoke with Harper in spring 2024, she had just received her last $850 monthly check from a local basic income program and started a full-time teaching role. This summer, she's back to working multiple jobs as a single parent, but feels much more confident about the future.

Harper is one of thousands of Americans who have participated in guaranteed basic income programs. The model — heralded by advocates as a solution to poverty and housing insecurity in big cities — offers no-strings-attached cash to low-income households, typically for one to three years.

Business Insider has spoken with dozens of participants and pilot leaders across the country. Most recipients put the money toward rent, groceries, childcare, and emergency expenses. A handful spend the funds on higher education or job training to further their careers.

Tech leaders like Sam Altman and Elon Musk — alongside several left-leaning lawmakers — have previously advocated basic income pilots, especially in a job market increasingly reshaped by AI. But it it can be difficult to maintain the political will and budget to run the programs sustainably, and participants have shared mixed results about their long-term impact.

Participant data for these pilots is collected before, during, and immediately after receiving payments. What's less documented is how households fare in the years after their deposits stop. The jury's out on whether short-term financial support translates to long-term stability.

"That money helped me get my daughter to college, it helped me keep my kids out of trouble," Harper said. "It's not just a handout. It can change a person's life."

Do you have a story to share about guaranteed basic income or cost of living? Reach out to this reporter at allisonkelly@businessinsider.com.

Taniquewa Brewster, 41, has a new baby. The little girl she adopted babbles as she does chores around the apartment, or takes calls for work as an assistant property manager.

Brewster first spoke with Business Insider in fall 2024, soon after receiving $12,000 over one year from a GBI program in Austin. At the time, the mother of five was working overtime and barely covering essentials, which she said was "keeping me away from my family."

Part of the draw with basic income is the element of choice. Other social safety nets, like SNAP or Medicaid, are restricted to specific purposes, with households only able to spend the money on groceries or healthcare. With cash, advocates say that participants have more agency. They can cover a car repair, buy school supplies for their kids, or pay down debt.

Several basic income participants told Business Insider that being able to use the extra cash for childcare and education allowed them to forgo unstable, part-time jobs in favor of a more lucrative full-time job. Others said the money helped them afford a security deposit for an apartment, or pay for their child to participate in a sport. For some, it eased the burden of medical bills.

The vast majority of participants reported that cash increased their food and housing security, as well as their mental health and parent-child time, according to research from 27 US pilots across published by the nonprofit Mayors for a Guaranteed Income at the end of last year.

In June, Brewster said she earned the certifications she needed for a promotion with the help of basic income. She's on her way to "breaking the curse of generational poverty" for her children, she said, and feels stable about her housing situation for the first time in a while.

"It felt like people were actually asking me what my needs were, and how they could help me meet those needs," Brewster added. "There's something comforting about someone actually caring enough to ask."

It's been five years since Crystal Crawford lost her job as a social worker, and she's getting back on her feet. She said she participated in Georgia basic income program, which gave her $500 a month between December 2021 and 2022. The money helped her cover bills and boost her professional certifications. The 40-year-old has a new job as a community engagement specialist, and a business strategy side hustle.

"Having the flexibility to be able to pay for things — like being able to get your hair done for a potential interview — guaranteed income allowed me to do things that I probably would not have been able to do during that time," she said, adding that "financial hardship can happen to anyone."

Basic income hasn't been a magic fix for Crawford's financial concerns. She said she has student loan debt in deferment and hopes to start making payments soon. And the balance of her savings account is "definitely not where I want it to be."

Other former participants shared a similar sentiment with Business Insider. Some felt cash payments helped with short-term bills and professional development, but most pilots didn't run long enough to impact their longer-term finances. Many said their savings accounts and retirement outlook didn't materially improve. A few, but not all, said their annual earnings rose because of their career growth.

There are also hurdles to running a basic income program in the first place — let alone one that lasts longer than a few years. Some tech leaders who previously championed GBI for displaced workers have walked back their stance, saying that the payoff doesn't justify the investment. Critics of basic income also worry that no-string-attached cash could discourage participants from working, or that the taxpayer cost is too high alongside other safety net programs like Medicaid and SNAP.

The cost of running these programs typically falls on local governments and philanthropists, and cities often aren't able to maintain lasting political will to keep GBI funded, with some lawmakers worried they aren't broadly effective.

Harper plans to keep working part-time on top of her full-time teaching job for her own peace of mind. Years after her cash payments ended, she said one income simply isn't enough to raise a family.

Still, she credits GBI for helping her recover from one of the toughest times in her life.

"Before basic income, I was pretty much homeless," Harper said. "I was able to get a new apartment, substitute teach, and pay my rent because I had that extra income. Later, it led me to get a bigger apartment, and land an even better job."

title: China hits travel platform Trip.com with $765M in penalties over monopoly abuses
description: China said on Saturday it had imposed penalties of nearly 5.2 billion yuan ($765 million) on Trip.com Group, which operates the country’s largest online travel platform, over claims of monopolistic conduct.  Trip.com, which runs Ctrip and Skyscanner among other brands, was said to be restricting market competition through means such as entering into exclusive partnerships with some hotels and offering prioritized traffic allocation to them, China’s State Administration for Market Regulation said in a statement.
fullText:
BEIJING (AP) — China said on Saturday it had imposed penalties of nearly 5.2 billion yuan ($765 million) on Trip.com Group, which operates the country's largest online travel platform, over claims of monopolistic conduct.

Trip.com, which runs Ctrip and Skyscanner among other brands, was said to be restricting market competition through means such as entering into exclusive partnerships with some hotels and offering prioritized traffic allocation to them, China's State Administration for Market Regulation said in a statement.

How much did China fine Trip.com for antitrust violations?

What market restrictions did Trip.com impose on hotels?

How did Trip.com respond to China's regulatory penalties?

What monopolistic practices did Trip.com allegedly engage in?

It prohibited some hotels from collaborating with competing platforms, the regulator added, and had also demanded some hotel operators who were operating on multiple platforms to ensure the rates for their platform were the lowest available online.

The regulator said Trip.com had been abusing its dominant market position in the sector since as early as 2020.

The regulator, which started its investigation against Trip.com in January, said it had confiscated "illegal gains" of more than 1.6 billion yuan ($245 million) from the group and had imposed a fine of over 3.5 billion yuan ($520 million).

The company was also asked to refund about 122 million yuan ($18 million) which it was withholding from hotel operators.

Trip.com's behavior had "eliminated and restricted market competition, constrained hotel operators from conducting cross-platform business, infringed upon hotel operators' right to set their own prices and harmed consumer interests," the regulator's statement said.

Trip.com acknowledged the decision in a statement Saturday, adding that it "sincerely accepts and will resolutely comply" with the penalties.

"(We will) systematically implement the rectification measures item-by-item and ensure their full execution," the group said.

title: Displaced from wildfires in Spain share their stories of uncertainty and narrow escapes
description: VILLAVICIOSA DE ODÓN, Spain (AP) — Elvira Menéndez knows how lucky she is that her house is not a charred ruin like so many others in Spain and France devastated by deadly wildfires.  The wildfires th...
fullText:
VILLAVICIOSA DE ODÓN, Spain (AP) — Elvira Menéndez knows how lucky she is that her house is not a charred ruin like so many others in Spain and France devastated by deadly wildfires.

But the 79-year-old retiree can't help but worry for another family that, like her, fled the raging inferno.

"They have been left with nothing," said about a young family that lives down her son's street. "The house has completely burned down, and they have three children."

The wildfires that have raged out of control in recent days in three provinces in central Spain have ravaged tens of thousands of hectares and forced nearly 90,000 people to flee their homes. In the southwest of France, more than 250,000 people have fled their homes as the fire rages through the wine region of Bordeaux.

For the hundreds of thousands of people in this situation, the question is the same: What will they find when they're finally allowed to go home, or to what's left of it?

With no word on when she'll be able to return to Chapinería, her hometown west of the Spanish capital of Madrid, Menéndez will spend her third night on Sunday at the makeshift shelter set up in a sports complex in Villaviciosa de Odón, a 40-minute drive from the home she was forced to leave as the blaze neared.

"At least we're all together," said Menéndez, who is at the shelter with her family and their dog.

On Friday afternoon, two major fires near Madrid merged into a single, rapidly spreading blaze. It later combined with another that was already burning in Ávila, north of the capital. This forced the government to declare a national fire emergency for the first time. Since then, the flames have also spread to Toledo, a province southwest. In all, the flames have scorched 77,000 hectares in the central part of the country alone.

Menéndez's anguish was shared by Rocío Domínguez, who fled her house with only the clothes on her back. "All the clothes, all the memories, everything, everything, everything," were left behind, she told The Associated Press.

"The only thing I had time to grab was a kit I have for the dogs," Domínguez added, surrounded by her two beloved pets. Everything else she has with her now — from the clothes she wears to her food and toiletries — she received at the shelter.

At the evacuation center, where cots have been set up for about 200 people, Domínguez still has the terrifying memory of their escape fresh in her mind.

"It was madness with cars going up and down, traffic jams in the village streets as people tried to get out. It looked like the apocalypse," told Domínguez, 35 years old and unemployed, who is with her parents and siblings. "You couldn't see anything."

"Everything was covered in ash," she added. "You could see all the burned animals."

Spanish King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia heard more of those personal testimonies on Sunday as the royals visited another shelter in Villamartín, about 45 kilometers west of Madrid.

And those stories may not be the last — Spain's Minister of Ecological Transition, Sara Aagesen, later noted that "more evacuations are still expected" in that area.

Queen Letizia told reporters after meeting with the survivors that it was important "to hear how they feel and how they recount their hasty departure from their home. How they have felt the sadness they describe, the anguish, the uncertainty, and those questions they leave hanging in the air,.

The wildfires have significantly shifted the mood in the country, where just a week ago huge crowds of people took to the streets to celebrate their second FIFA World Cup triumph.

As the echoes of those celebrations fade, head coach Luis de la Fuente — one of the driving forces behind the historic victory over Argentina in the final in New Jersey — visited those affected by the fires at a sports center in Las Rozas.

The Spanish Football Federation, which has its headquarters in the same city, has offered the facilities where the newly crowned world champions usually train for the vulnerable families who have been forced to evacuate from their homes.

The coach said all of Spain is rallying for the wildfire survivors.

"All of Spain is watching over them," De la Fuente said in remarks to the national public broadcaster, TVE. "They have the support of the entire country, the same support we have when we play soccer. It's exactly the same."

title: They thought they'd be retiring. Instead, they're grandparenting full time.
description: Vicki and Sal Parisella are among the many US grandparents sacrificing retirement and health to raise grandchildren and keep them out of foster care.
fullText:
It's not the way they thought they'd be spending their older years: getting two tweens ready for school and scraping together meals from food banks.

At the crack of dawn one Tuesday morning, 59-year-old Vicki Parisella bangs on her granddaughters' bedroom doors. Silence from Myaliissa's room; a whine from Tatiana's. Minutes later, Tatiana drags her backpack into the living room.

"Your shirt's on backward," Vicki tells the 11-year-old.

As if Vicki flipped an on-switch, Tatiana zooms around the living room while Vicki's husband, Sal, packs their lunches. Vicki braids Tatiana's hair and helps her put on her shoes as Myaliissa, 13, gets dressed. By 7:20, Vicki already has a headache.

Vicki and Sal, 76, are part of a growing population of 1.1 million US grandparents 60 and older who have returned to parenting roles when they expected to be retiring.

Business Insider has spoken to more than 50 grandparents in this position in recent months. They said they've taken up parenting duties because of a child's death, drug use, or health issues. They all said they would make the decision to raise their grandchildren again in a heartbeat, though with few resources, most agreed that every day brought new financial and emotional challenges.

Noah Sheidlower spoke with Vicki and Sal Parisella over the course of six months to learn how raising two of their granddaughters in Lakeland, Florida, has changed their lives. He visited them for two days and reviewed financial, court, and medical records for this story. If you would like to share your story about grandparenting in America, fill out this quick form, and 

The new reality of being a grandparent

I'm 63 and raising four of my grandchildren. I haven't once thought about retiring.

I'm 73 and raising 3 great-grandchildren. Money is tight — I had to unretire to support my family.

Like many of the grandparents who spoke to Business Insider, Vicki and Sal rarely have enough money to make it through the month. Vicki, who's the sole breadwinner due to Sal's kidney condition, overdrew her bank account paying rent earlier this year. The family gets most of its meals from food banks. In July, they got an eviction notice they're disputing.

But all that can wait for later. For now, Vicki has to get the kids to school.

"We're going to be late. Run to the car," Vicki shouts.

Tatiana sprints, her lunchbox flopping by her side. Myaliissa follows, not saying a word.

After dropping the girls at school, Vicki lights a cigarette. She calls Sal as she winds through traffic in her 2023 Toyota Camry on the way to her accounts payable job.

"I caught the freaking train," she tells Sal as she gets stuck at a crossing. She arrives at her desk with 30 seconds to spare. Crisis averted this time, she says, knowing full well the train could ruin her morning tomorrow.

Vicki can't afford to risk her job, which nets her $615 a week. Sal receives $1,435 monthly in Social Security. It's enough for the family to break even, unless something breaks or someone gets sick.

US Census data in 2024 showed that more than 3 million children lived in households with grandparents who had some responsibility for their care. To avoid the foster care system and give their grandchildren a shot at promising futures, some grandparents have sacrificed their financial security, retirements, social life, and physical and mental well-being.

"What's going to happen to them if I die, since I don't want them in foster care?" Rebecca Black, 63, said she frequently asks herself as a grandmother raising two grandsons in Texas. Black said she's been financially strained, but retired so she could be more present in their lives.

Madalyn Conchola, 62, said that her four granddaughters, ages 7 through 19, struggled after she adopted them. With few financial or community support resources, most of her $70,000 annual salary, plus a small state subsidy, goes toward raising them. Five years and lots of hard work later, she said her granddaughters have all been thriving in school.

"As time goes on, my age and my ability to work and earn money loom over me," said Conchola, in Arizona. "I'm looking for other ways to try to generate an income."

It's a concern that has plagued Vicki and Sal. They've had temporary custody of their granddaughters since their daughter Siobhan's relationship fell apart in 2017. The 36-year-old still sees the girls, but said she hasn't been able to get back on her feet to raise them full time.

"I do feel bad because of the burden of everything they have, but there's nothing really that I can do right now about it until I move closer," says Siobhan, who lives in Tampa.

That year, the family was evicted from their three-bedroom home in Lakeland because they couldn't afford the $1,143 rent. They moved to a Salvation Army shelter and were able to get by with assistance from her coworkers and Vicki's sister, Nicole Spottke.

"They're both incredibly patient. They get frustrated, as would anyone who's exhausted does, but the girls are raised really well," said Spottke, 55. "Vicki would like to be able to give them more financially, but truly, I wish she'd get it through her head that the time that she gives to the kids — that's so much more important."

After two years, they were able to rent a home with a small pool, enough room for the girls to run around, and a quiet space for Vicki to decompress. The house wasn't without its problems —mold, flooding, and broken appliances — but for five years, it did the job. Vicki said their lives slowly improved.

When that house sold two years ago, they saw a huge rent spike when securing their next home — to $2,075 monthly, leaving them with $725 less to spend on everything else — food, clothes for the girls, and gas. They often come up short. Their backyard is covered with weeds, their front lawn is uneven, and the house is old, but unable to find any other place in their budget, they renewed their lease.

"We know there are people worse off than us, but I need to vent because I'm frustrated," Vicki says in her dark living room. She keeps the lights off to save electricity.

As she drives to pick up the girls, Vicki pauses at a stoplight and lets out a sigh. Every minute and every dollar matters, she says. Still, she tries not to push her frustrations onto her granddaughters.

"If the girls were taken from us, I would lose it because I'd be worried constantly," Vicki says, crossing over two lanes of traffic.

Vicki and Sal have been unable to permanently adopt their grandchildren because their father hasn't signed over his rights. If they challenged him in court, lawyers told them it could prompt him to try to regain custody, and they could lose the girls

Other grandparents told Business Insider how they have struggled to secure permanent parental rights. Though policies vary by state, the parents must generally relinquish their parental rights first, or grandparents must prove that the parents are unable or unwilling to care for their child — often due to neglect, incarceration, or severe illness — while showing that granting custody is in the child's best interest.

The complicated legal process often leaves grandparents with little financial assistance while raising their grandchildren because they often don't qualify for the same benefits as foster parents. Business Insider spoke with some grandparents who spent as much as $70,000 to secure legal custody.

Carol Leonard, 65, decided not to go to court to get custody of her two teenage grandsons in Louisiana. She can't afford an attorney; the last one she spoke with requested $800 upfront. Because the father's parental rights have not been terminated, he would be able to petition the court to regain custody. Still, she's been able to enroll them in school and get them medical care.

Siobhan, the girls' mother, said she is willing to relinquish her parental rights. She said she calls Myaliissa and Tatiana frequently. She lives with her fiancé and works in retail. Siobhan also lost custody of her two other children, who live with her fiancé's parents.

"I of course know them, but I don't really know them," Siobhan says of her daughters. "I could name a few things that they like and what they're into, but I don't know everything."

Vicki and Sal still hope they'll be able to adopt the girls someday, though they know the road will be long and tiring. Would they change anything about the lengths they've taken to protect the girls? "No freaking way," Vicki says.

Running late to pick up the girls from school, Vicki hurls her purse over her shoulder and gives Sal a kiss. She gets into her car, which they bought in January after their previous one was repossessed. It's been years since she's gotten her nails done or gone to the dentist. She's upped her anxiety medications. They've discussed bankruptcy with their lawyer.

Myaliissa and Tatiana both attend private school because their grandparents wanted an education infused with Christian values. Tuition is covered by scholarships; uniforms cost an extra $300 a year for both girls. On a recent report card, Tatiana got five As — and a Krispy Kreme doughnut from the school for each. For years, Myaliissa was chatty and animated, but she's recently gone back into her shell.

Children who have lived through adverse experiences with their birth parents are at increased risk for physical, developmental, and behavioral challenges, said Carol Musil, who spent years studying grandparents who served as primary caregivers while at Case Western Reserve University in Ohio. Her research shows that applies to caregivers as well; grandmothers raising grandchildren often have worse physical health, depressive symptoms, and stress compared to other grandmothers.

Tatiana and Myaliissa have missed out on some staples of childhood, including summer camp and most after-school activities. Yvette Lovell, Myaliissa's godmother, who has taught both girls at school, says the Parisellas are "salt-of-the-earth kind of people" who don't have enough support. She's seen Vicki and Sal make tough sacrifices, including shielding them from family drama.

"I've been in education for almost 40 years, and I can count the number of grandparents who have taken on being the core for the grandchildren as they have," Lovell says.

Back home from school, as the night progresses, Tatiana becomes restless. She'd like to stay up an hour later, running around the house, tickling Vicki and Sal. She grabs the family's photo book and heads to her room. Myaliissa drags her blanket through the hallway to her room.

Tatiana grabs the book and looks through it as Vicki and Sal get her ready for bed. She sees snapshots of the family's trip to Disney World and the time when they all put their feet in the ocean at Cocoa Beach. Absent are photos of the times Vicki shielded the girls from flooding, the court documents that determined their futures, and the tough conversations the grandparents had about whether to buy milk or pay the electricity bill.

For now, all that matters is those genuine smiles on the last page, conveying joy that, if only for a day here and there, keeps them going.

"We want you to have that when we're not around anymore," Vicki tells her, reaching for a hug. "We want you to remember and say, 'Grandma and Grandpa took good care of me.'"

If you enjoyed this story, be sure to follow Business Insider on Yahoo.

title: Appeals court upholds injunction on President Trump’s mail-in voting order
description: A federal appeals court on Saturday ruled against the Trump administration’s efforts to implement stricter mail-in voting rules before midterm elections in the coming months, with control of both the ...
fullText:
A federal appeals court on Saturday ruled against the Trump administration's efforts to implement stricter mail-in voting rules before midterm elections in the coming months, with control of both the House and Senate up for grabs.

The 1st U.S. Circuit of Appeals declined to lift a lower-court injunction from June that ruled parts of President Trump's order was unconstitutional after Democratic-led states, including California, Massachusetts and Washington, sued the administration.

The appeals court rejected the administration's appeal in a 2-1 decision.

The Trump order directed the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to put together a list of confirmed U.S. citizens eligible to vote in each state. The list would be made using sensitive citizenship data from federal databases. The order also directed the Department of Justice (DOJ) to investigate officials who mail ballots to people who are "not eligible" to vote.

Talwani, in her ruling, said Trump had no authority to have the DHS to compile this data and the USPS equally had no authority to follow these orders about mail-in voting. She added that Trump had no power  "to intimidate local election officials to use the necessarily incomplete confirmed citizenship lists as a resource, lest they face criminal prosecution."

Trump has remained critical of mail-in ballots and in his July primetime address on election integrity said there were "shocking vulnerabilities in our election infrastructure. This evidence shows that the election system we have dangerously exposes, and really exposes like levels never thought possible, the hacking, exploitation, and foreign interference."

He also mentioned in the same speech that how long it took California to count mail-in ballots was "one example of insanity" caused by mail-in voting.

The Department of Justice (DOJ) has said that absent any ruling in its favor the administration may ask the U.S. Supreme Court to intervene.

title: Why rattlesnake bites in California are surging
description: Rattlesnake bites are climbing in California, and officials say an unusually active season is helping drive the surge.
fullText:
(NewsNation) — California is seeing an unusual rise in rattlesnake bites in 2026.

Health officials are reporting encounters occurring earlier and more frequently than normal, according to NewsNation affiliate KTLA.

The California Poison Control System has logged more than 250 rattlesnake-related calls so far in 2026.

For comparison, the agency typically receives about 200 such calls during an entire year.

Three deaths have been linked to venomous snake bites in California this year:

Feb. 1: Julian Hernandez, 25, died after being bitten while mountain biking at Quail Hill Trailhead in Irvine.

March 14: Gabriela Bautista, 46, died five days after being bitten while hiking at Wildwood Regional Park in Thousand Oaks.

April 8: A 78-year-old woman died two days after being bitten multiple times on rural property in Redwood Valley. Officials have not confirmed which species bit her.

Rais Vohra, medical director for the Fresno/Madera Division of the California Poison Control System, told KTLA that the death toll is "highly unusual and deeply concerning."

He said California typically records about one rattlesnake-related death per year.

Officials say recent heat waves are a key factor. Rattlesnakes generally avoid people, but encounters become more likely as more people spend time outdoors during warmer weather.

The California Poison Control System typically receives the most calls between April and October. However, a spring heat wave that began in early March accelerated snake emergence, according to the Biothreats Emergence, Analysis and Communications Network.

According to BEACON, earlier and warmer weather is increasing rattlesnake activity across parts of the West, including some areas of Colorado. The California Poison Control System recommends:

Carry a fully charged phone and hike with a companion.

Tell someone where you're hiking and when you expect to return.

Stay on clear trails and avoid tall grass and dense brush.

Check logs and rocks for camouflaged rattlesnakes before sitting down.

Avoid wearing earphones so you can hear warning rattles, though snakes do not always rattle before striking.

Listen for faint buzzing or hissing sounds.

If you encounter a rattlesnake, back away slowly and give it space. A rattlesnake can strike from up to half its body length away. If bitten, call 911 immediately and seek medical attention.

title: My entire family went on a boat trip that they never returned from
description: Peter Watts was just 14 when a pleasure boat disaster killed 15 people, including his entire family.
fullText:
"It's something you don't get over - you learn to live with it."

Sixty years ago, Peter Watts' entire family was killed in a boating tragedy that shocked the nation.

His nine-year-old sister Angela, 10-year-old brother David, mother Doreen and father Frederick George, along with 11 others, died when the Prince of Wales pleasure boat sank on the Mawddach Estuary in Gwynedd on 22 July, 1966.

Now, a memorial recalling the names of the 15 people who lost their lives has been unveiled.

It was another chance for Peter to travel from the village he grew up in, near Milton Keynes, to the picturesque estuary where the catastrophe unfolded.

"We'd been on holidays in previous years and I'd been on this boat trip [before] and I didn't want to go again," Peter recalled.

Peter was 14 at the time, old enough to be allowed to spend the day on his own in the seaside town of Barmouth, where his family were staying in a boarding house.

The rest of his family joined the queue to board the Prince of Wales for the eight mile (13km) trip down the estuary to the George III Hotel at Penmaenpool.

But the tide pushed the ferry boat into the Penmaenpool toll bridge across the estuary, flinging the 42 passengers into the water as the vessel was wrecked on the bridge.

Local people, including the hotel owner and staff and the toll bridge keeper, ran to the aid of those in the water, managing to pull 27 to safety.

But along with Peter's brother and sister, two other children were among the 15 who could not be saved.

"This happened in the morning, at about 11 in the morning, and I was just waiting hours and hours for them to come back - and they didn't come back," said Peter.

"I went down to the harbour and I heard two people talking about a boat that had sunk. I asked them what was going on, and they said what it was, and I said 'My family is on it' - and they said 'Go to the police station'.

"I sat in there for what seemed ever and a day, and they took the details."

The guest house owners came to take him back, while his aunt and uncle drove up to be with him.

"The next morning we went to Dolgellau to the hospital, where they had found three of them - my mother was still missing," he said.

"My father could swim, but my uncle who identified him said he had had a nasty blow on his head."

It would be another three days before his mother's body was found.

An official inquiry found the boat was carrying six more passengers than the maximum 36 permitted under its certification.

There should also have been two crew members - one on the engine and one on the rudder.

But there was only skipper Edward Llewelyn, 73 at the time, who was found to have acted negligently by a Board of Trade inquiry.

The boat was also short of lifebelts and buoyancy apparatus was stowed away.

Llewelyn was ordered to pay £100 towards the inquiry costs, but no prosecutions were ever brought.

However, the inquiry did lead to changes in the law governing insurance and the number of passengers boats could carry.

The events have left a deep mark on Peter, and the urge to return to Barmouth and the estuary as often as he could.

"If I've ever been anywhere near Wales, even when I've been going to Holyhead, when we went to Ireland, I'd come round this way," he said.

Returning this time on the 60th anniversary of the tragedy, it was marked with a special memorial and the plaque to remember those who died, unveiled by Dolgellau Town Council.

"Those 15 people - I didn't want them to be forgotten. Having their names there - that's what I wanted," said Peter.

title: Traveling to Hawaii this week? What Hurricane Fausto means for your trip
description: Hurricane Fausto is expected to pass near Hawaii early this week. Here's what travelers should know about the forecast track, dangerous surf and flights.
fullText:
Hurricane Fausto is on track to pass near Hawaii early this week. Forecasters expect it to weaken before it arrives, but the storm is worrying for anyone with a trip to the islands. Here is what travelers should know.

As of the National Hurricane Center's 5 p.m. Hawaii time update Saturday, Fausto was a Category 2 hurricane with 100 mph winds, centered about 1,060 miles east of Hilo and moving west at 13 mph. It was forecast to cross into the central Pacific on Sunday and weaken from there.

Probably not directly. The latest forecast track carries Fausto just north of the islands on Tuesday and Wednesday as a weakening tropical storm, with winds down around 45 mph. Forecasters say the strongest winds and heaviest rain are likely to stay offshore to the north, though a small shift in the track could change that. No coastal watches or warnings were in effect Sunday.

The clearest impact is in the water. The hurricane center said swells from Fausto will reach the islands well ahead of the storm, building on east-facing shores of the eastern islands starting Sunday and spreading west into Monday and Tuesday. Those swells are expected to bring life-threatening surf and strong rip currents. On Oahu, state officials closed the trailhead to the Makapuu tidepools as a precaution.

Flights were running normally on Sunday. Hawaiian Airlines, the islands' largest carrier, reported just one cancellation across its network Sunday, according to FlightAware, and no Hawaii airport was among those with significant delays. The airline had not issued a travel waiver for Fausto, and the U.S. Coast Guard set Port Condition Whiskey for all Hawaii commercial ports as a precaution. Anyone flying to or from the islands this week should still watch for airline alerts.

Monitor your airline and the National Weather Service in Honolulu for updates.

Stay out of the water on east- and south-facing shores, and heed lifeguard and closure signs.

If you are staying in a coastal or flood-prone area, learn your evacuation zone.

Officials are urging residents to keep at least a 14-day supply of food, water and medication on hand during hurricane season.

Fausto is the first hurricane to move into the central Pacific this season. A Hurricane Hunter aircraft was scheduled to fly into the storm Sunday to sharpen the forecast.

title: De Klerk holds nerve as Spirit edge past Rockets
description: South African all-rounder Nadine de Klerk stars with 41 not out from 22 balls as London Spirit beat Trent Rockets with three balls to spare.
fullText:
The Hundred women's competition, Trent Bridge

Trent Rockets 142-7 (100 balls): Gardner 34 (22); Kapp 3-12

London Spirit 146-5 (97 balls): De Klerk 41* (22); Gardner 2-24

London Spirit won by five wickets

All-rounder Nadine de Klerk held her nerve to lead London Spirit to a tense five-wicket win over Trent Rockets with three balls to spare.

Chasing 143 at Trent Bridge, Spirit were in trouble at 67-4 after losing four wickets for 12 runs and were in danger of wasting their positive start from opener Grace Harris' knock of 37 from 20 balls.

But De Klerk and Marie Kelly combined for a counter-attacking stand of 63 from 37 balls to propel Spirit to their first win of the season.

With power-hitter Deandra Dottin waiting in the dugout, there was some concern about Kelly's slow start as she stuttered to 12 from 13 balls, but she impressively kicked on to score 39 from 26 deliveries.

After her departure with 13 still needed to win, Rockets' bowlers fought to take the game deep but De Klerk - who has made a name for herself as a finisher in the past couple of years - whacked two sixes in the last four balls in a nerveless knock of 41 not out from 22 balls.

Earlier, De Klerk's fellow South African Marizanne Kapp had set the tone with the ball for Spirit with a fine spell of 3-12.

Kapp bowled Beth Mooney first ball before removing Sophia Dunkley and Sophie Luff, but Ash Gardner's 34 and a dynamic 31 off 19 balls from Bess Heath led Rockets' recovery to 142-7.

Gardner was caught on the boundary off England's Charlie Dean, who also impressed with 2-18, which allowed Spirit to keep the run-rate under control as Heath struggled for support from the lower order.

Both teams have one win from two so far, but Rockets are more comfortable at third in the table with a superior net run-rate.

The earlier match between Manchester Super Giants and Birmingham Phoenix was abandoned without a ball bowled at Old Trafford.

title: Middlesex and Worcs extend 100% One-Day Cup starts
description: Middlesex and holders Worcestershire achieve contrasting wins to extend their perfect starts to this year's One-Day Cup.
fullText:
Middlesex and holders Worcestershire achieved contrasting wins to extend their perfect starts to this year's One-Day Cup.

Eight group matches were played on Sunday, with Worcestershire clinching a dramatic four-run victory in the final over against Hampshire.

But Middlesex again caught the eye with another dominant performance, dismissing Glamorgan for just 66 and then requiring only 9.1 overs to reach their victory target.

Middlesex are the only side to have won their first three matches, while Worcestershire are one of three teams to have won two out of two.

Elsewhere, former England Test batters Keaton Jennings and Tom Westley struck centuries in wins for Lancashire and Essex respectively, while Ben Coad claimed a maiden five-wicket haul in white-ball cricket as Yorkshire thrashed Sussex.

One-Day Cup results, scorecards and fixtures

Leicestershire's winning start came to an end in a high-scoring meeting with Lancashire at Grace Road.

Jennings starred with 135 off 134 balls as the visitors posted 383-4 and, in reply, the Foxes were reduced to 22-4 before a 179-run fifth-wicket partnership between Hamza Shaikh (91) and Ruan de Swardt (126) brought the hosts back into contention.

Despite the Foxes taking the match into the final over, Lancashire held on for their first win by a 21-run margin.

Cameron Bancroft (89 not out) and James Bracey (83) scored half-centuries as Gloucestershire also claimed their first victory of the campaign with a six-wicket win over Kent in Bristol.

The hosts' success owed much to a strong performance in the field as seamers Will Williams and Luke Charlesworth returned figures of 3-33 and 3-42 respectively to help dismiss Kent for 208.

Warwickshire are now the only Group A side yet to register a victory in this year's competition after a comprehensive 125-run defeat by Somerset at Taunton.

Somerset captain Lewis Goldsworthy (103) led from the front with his third List A century as last year's beaten semi-finalists scored 337-8.

In reply, Warwickshire were bowled out for 212, with 19-year-old seamer James Theedom claiming 4-54 in what was only his third List A appearance.

Elsewhere in Group A, Surrey eased to a six-wicket win over T20 Blast winners Northamptonshire Steelbacks in Guildford.

Benji Floros took 4-60 as the Steelbacks ended on 254-8, but Surrey had little trouble chasing their target, with Adam Thomas ending on 83 not out as they won with almost seven overs to spare.

Worcestershire appeared to be cruising towards victory when Hampshire, chasing 308, needed 48 runs to win with 21 balls remaining and one wicket in hand.

Some big hitting from Andrew Neal took Hampshire to the brink of an astonishing success but, requiring five more off the final three balls, he edged spinner Fateh Singh behind to fall for 48 off 22 balls.

The late drama at New Road was in sharp contrast to events earlier in the day at Radlett, where Middlesex made short work of Glamorgan's batting line-up.

Naavya Sharma (4-29), Toby Roland-Jones (3-35) and Noah Cornwell (3-1) were the only three bowlers used as Glamorgan, who were 44-1, lost their final nine wickets for 22 runs.

Josh de Caires hit 10 fours in his 45 not out as the hosts completed victory within three hours of the match starting.

At Hove, an early rain shower meant a slightly reduced match of 48 overs per side.

Opener Will Luxton made 117 in Yorkshire's 325-7 and Coad's four wickets with the new ball left Sussex on 21-5 as they chased a revised target of 325.

Coad ended with 5-12 from seven overs as Sussex were bowled out for 140 to lose by 184 runs on the DLS method.

Essex beat Derbyshire by nine runs at Chelmsford in the other match in Group B, with both captains leading their sides' respective batting causes.

Westley, making his 500th career appearance in all formats, scored 102 off 97 balls in the hosts' 257-7.

Harry Came (97) shared an opening stand of 113 with Martin Andersson but the match looked in the balance when Derbyshire needed 100 more with five wickets in hand.

Charlie Bennett (3-32) broke a seventh-wicket partnership worth 45 between Ross Whiteley and Nick Potts, which proved crucial.

title: England suffer heavy netball defeat by Australia
description: England captain Fran Williams says her team were "far from our best" in a 66-47 defeat by defending Commonwealth champions Australia.
fullText:
England captain Fran Williams said her team were "far from our best" in a heavy defeat by defending Commonwealth champions Australia.

The Roses opened their campaign in Pool A with a 83-34 victory over Northern Ireland on Saturday.

But they were outplayed on Sunday as Australia cruised to a 66-47 win at The Hydro in Glasgow.

"That's not the result we came for and not the performance," Williams told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"We didn't cope well with their physicality. It's really tough when a game blows out like that."

Australia started strongly, racing into an 18-11 lead after the first quarter and extending their advantage to 56-35 by the end of the third.

Sophie Garbin scored 41 goals from 42 attempts for Australia, while Olivia Tchine was England's highest scorer with 23 from 25.

England face Malawi at 14:00 BST on Monday.

Earlier on Sunday, Scotland picked up their first win in Pool B with a 56-47 victory over Wales.

England, who won gold in 2018, failed to make the podium at Birmingham 2022.

Only two of the 12 players in the squad - Eleanor Cardwell and Imogen Allison - have experience in the Commonwealth Games after injuries to gold medallists Helen Housby and Natalie Metcalf, who withdrew with a calf injury on Monday.

Jess Thirlby stepped down as head coach in March for family reasons, leaving assistant Anna Stembridge - head coach from 2011 to 2015 - in interim charge.

Northern Ireland fell to their second Pool A defeat as they lost 64-48 to Malawi.

Malawi dominated the first quarter and raced into a 19-9 lead, with Northern Ireland struggling to match their intensity.

Sheonah Forbes' side improved in the second quarter, but Malawi finished strongly to move 35-23 ahead by the half-time break.

The Warriors managed to outscore Malawi in a much more competitive third quarter as they narrowed the gap to 44-38.

But a sharper Malawi outfit pulled further away in the final quarter as they picked up their first win.

Goal shooter Mwayi Kumwenda scored 58 goals from the 59 shots she attempted.

Northern Ireland will be back in action against Tonga on Monday at 16:00.

title: Shin holds on to win Women's Scottish Open
description: Jenny Shin survives a tricky final round to see off fellow South Korean A-Lim Kim and win the Women's Scottish Open.
fullText:
Women's Scottish Open final leaderboard

-9 J Shin (Kor); -7 A Kim (Kor); -5 P Anannarukarn (Tha); -4 E Henseleit (Ger); -3 L Coughlin (US), M Yamashita (Jpn); -2 C Wannasaen (Tha)

Selected others: -1 L Maguire (Ire); +2 N Korda (US); +10 C Hull (Eng)

Jenny Shin survived a tricky final round to see off fellow South Korean A-Lim Kim and win the Women's Scottish Open at Dundonald.

Shin hit three bogeys on the front nine in a three-over-par 75 to finish on nine under.

Kim, who carded a fine 68, was two shots behind, with Thailand's Pajaree Anannarukarn a further two strokes back in third.

It was Shin's first title in more than 10 years and only her second on the LPGA Tour in 368 attempts.

She was in tears after the final putt dropped on the 18th and was doused with water and champagne by a group of friends.

"My first one didn't really feel like a win at the time," said Shin, whose debut title came at the Volunteers of America Texas Shootout in 2016.

"I didn't feel like I deserved it. It felt very accidental.

"But this one definitely feels a lot different. This one feels like I earned it. I worked hard for it."

Only 10 players broke par after four rounds, with England's Charley Hull finishing on 10 over after a round of 74.

American Nelly Korda, who has won two of the four majors played this year, went round in 69 for a share of 16th on two over.

The final major of the year, the Women's Open at Royal Lytham and St Annes in Lancashire, starts on Thursday.

"We experienced everything this week - sunshine, a little bit of warmth, and sideways rain, gusty winds, but that's a given out here," said Korda.

"So [I am] just trying to get into the mindset for next week. There's so many things that are going on during your shot that you really have to stay committed."

title: Maynard loses York job three months after dramatic title win
description: York City confirm the exit of manager Stuart Maynard, three months after he guided the club back into the English Football League.
fullText:
York City have announced the exit of manager Stuart Maynard, three months after he guided the club back into the English Football League after a 10-year absence.

A club statement, external posted on social media said it had "not been an easy decision" by the board and it was made because of a "difference in direction and vision for the football club".

York won the National League in dramatic circumstances in April, scoring an equaliser in the 13th minute of second-half stoppage time to draw with title rivals Rochdale - who would have been champions themselves had they won.

The Minstermen ended the campaign on 108 points, having replaced Adam Hinshelwood with former Notts County boss Maynard in August 2025.

The statement continued: "We recognise that, from the outside, this may look like a strange or difficult decision to understand.

"But we believe that in the long term, the football club will be in a stronger position because of it, another step towards the vision we, as custodians of this club, believe will deliver sustained success."

It added: "We hope our track record of improving year on year has earned us a degree of trust and we understand that not everyone will agree with, or fully understand, this decision right away."

York host Crawley Town in a Carabao Cup preliminary-round tie on Monday, 3 August and their first League Two match of the season is a home fixture against Bristol Rovers 12 days later.

title: Buttler brilliance as Super Giants thump Phoenix
description: Jos Buttler produces a masterful 90 from 50 balls as Manchester Super Giants defeat Birmingham Phoenix to maintain their perfect start to The Hundred.
fullText:

Manchester Super Giants won by 87 runs

Jos Buttler produced a masterful 90 from 50 balls as Manchester Super Giants demolished Birmingham Phoenix by 87 runs to maintain their perfect start to The Hundred.

After scoring his highest T20 score of 131 against India earlier this month, the England wicketkeeper-batter continued his resurgence, striking seven fours and five sixes to lead the home side to 187-5.
